topic: Local Government Support Fund rationale, allocation, and monitoring
summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula and Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DILG's authority, monitoring role, transparency, and treatment of unused LGSF balances. DILG said DBM released and validated the assistance while DILG monitored distribution, implementation, and reports, and Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla committed to submit utilization reports covering 2025 and 2026. The agency defended the proposed LGSF of about 58 billion as supplemental funding because the national tax allotment was spread across many provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays. DILG described engineers, project evaluation officers, local monitoring committees, CSO and NGO participation, and the Subay Bayan portal as safeguards. A civil-society-backed line of questioning sought justification after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, evidence against duplication, open-data disclosure, participatory budgeting, and human-rights safeguards. DILG answered these questions in part, but the broader policy and accountability concerns remained open.
question: The committee sought to establish why a separate Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) remained necessary after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling increased LGUs' national tax allotment, what programs and fiscal gaps it addressed, and how funds were allocated, validated, implemented, monitored, and disclosed. Members also asked whether DILG or DBM controlled distribution and whether community participation and human-rights safeguards were adequate.
agency_position: DILG maintained that DBM controlled LGSF policy, validation, allocation, and release, while DILG monitored, evaluated, and reported on implementation. It defended LGSF as supplemental funding needed because the national tax allotment was divided among many LGUs and said safeguards included engineers, project monitoring officers, three-tier monitoring, local monitoring committees with CSO participation, reporting portals, and referral of confirmed wrongdoing.
outcome: DILG clarified that DBM controlled LGSF validation, policy, and release, while DILG monitored implementation and relied on COA and other monitoring mechanisms for accountability. The committee received commitments for utilization reports, but questions about the fund's discretionary structure, duplication with national tax allotments, unused prior-year balances, measurable outcomes, and independent safeguards were not fully resolved.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She asked DILG to confirm its role in administering and monitoring LGSF financial assistance to LGUs, including assistance for development projects and indigent individuals' education scholarships.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said DILG's sole function was to monitor distribution and present reports. DBM dispersed the money, while COA and DILG monitored its distribution.

thread.speaker: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula
thread.said: She asked whether DILG had received reports of similar problems in its monitoring of LGSF assistance.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said DILG had seen such reports and was monitoring them, but determining relationships between recipients and disbursement personnel was difficult. DILG remained open to investigating complaints submitted to it.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said confirmed wrongdoing would be referred to the relevant municipality or city authority, or, for more serious cases, to the Ombudsman.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He questioned DILG's role in implementing and monitoring LGSF financial assistance and noted that the proposal had grown from 5,000,000 in the NEP to 37,400,000,000 in the enacted budget process.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He asked whether DILG had a role in setting the DBM guidelines and distribution levels for financial assistance, including maximum amounts for Ayuda, medical assistance, and infrastructure.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said the guidelines were issued by DBM, not DILG. DILG was strictly a monitoring body and had no policy-making role in the distribution or utilization of the fund.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He cited the DBM guidelines allowing requests to be forwarded to DILG for a recommended amount for each LGU and asked whether this gave DILG discretion.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said DILG had received very few such referrals, which were handled by undersecretaries. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla added that the referrals mostly concerned water systems.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He cited a total 2026 LGSF of 50,000,000,000, more than PHP10 billion in continuing appropriations, for a total of PHP68 billion, and asked DILG to confirm.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla confirmed the figure. The member then stated that PHP57 billion was the 2026 figure and that PHP68 billion had been proposed for the following year.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: He said the utilization rate would be determined at year-end because the program started in 2026. DILG would provide a full report in 2027 after monitoring distribution and use.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He noted that LGUs were required to submit quarterly utilization reports to DBM, DILG, and Congress, and asked for updates covering 2025 and 2026.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla said DILG would submit the requested reports to the committee and undertook to submit them within the day.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: In response to a question on implementation, he stated that implementation was at 100%. He said DILG hired engineers to assess projects, while COA would be needed to determine whether more than 40,000 LGU recipients complied and achieved the required results.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He raised the guideline requiring a Certificate of Reversion for undisbursed balances from completed LGSF financial-assistance projects for fiscal years 2016 to 2025 and asked about unused funds.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla said the 2016 to 2025 period was under Congress's purview rather than DILG's distribution responsibility. He said DILG took full cognizance of the matter only in 2026.

thread.speaker: Rep. Antonio Tinio
thread.said: He expressed concern about transparency and the discretionary element of LGSF infrastructure assistance.

thread.speaker: Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla
thread.said: Secretary Remulla said LGU accountability requirements were stringent, including bids and awards committees, post-qualification, post-assessment, and review. He said DILG would file charges if discrepancies were identified.

thread.speaker: Anna York Bondoc
thread.said: She said she supported placing LGSF implementation under stronger DILG ground supervision rather than relying only on DBM monitoring. She also raised the absence of clear LGSF timelines and deadlines as an implementation concern.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: On behalf of civil society organizations, he asked why a separate LGSF was retained after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling expanded the national tax allotment, what fiscal gaps it addressed, and how the government ensured that it supplemented rather than duplicated regular LGU revenues.

thread.speaker: DILG official
thread.said: The official said the estimated 2027 national tax allotment was about one point three two to one point four billion trillion pesos, but it was divided among 82 provinces, 149 cities, 1,493 municipalities, and more than 42,000 barangays. The proposed LGSF of 58,000,000,000 was described as additional funding for water and sanitation systems, farm-to-market roads, electrification, health centers, and other basic services.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked DILG to clarify its role in LGSF monitoring, evaluation, implementation, and project validation.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said LGSF was released directly to LGUs, while DILG monitored, evaluated, and checked implementation. DILG had funding to hire engineers and project evaluation officers for deployment to provinces and regions.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked whether DBM handled the validation and vetting of LGU proposals and whether DILG ensured that projects were not duplicates.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said DBM created the portal where LGUs submitted project proposals and handled the validation and vetting. He agreed that DILG did not handle that process and that the question of duplication could be directed to DBM; LGUs identified their own priority projects.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked how local development councils, sanggunians, accredited CSOs, sectoral representatives, and affected communities participated in project identification, procurement, monitoring, and validation, and what outputs and disclosure requirements corresponded to the proposed monitoring allocation.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog described a three-tier monitoring system: local project monitoring committees composed of LGU officials and CSOs, DILG's second-party monitoring, and third-party monitoring involving CSOs and NGOs. He also cited the Subay Bayan portal, where LGUs were required to upload project status updates.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: He said 63,000,000 was allocated for monitoring and evaluation and 560,000,000 was used for salaries of engineers and project evaluation officers hired for field monitoring.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked what performance evidence supported the relative allocations for LGSF and participatory budgeting and how DILG would expand meaningful CSO and community participation throughout the project cycle.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said the Support to Barangay Development Program addressed basic-service gaps in barangays previously influenced by communist armed groups, while participatory-budgeting assistance funded water systems and evacuation centers identified through consultations. He said the latter had a 1,000,000,000 allocation in 2026.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked what safeguards prevented LGSF and SBDP projects from exposing CSOs, human-rights defenders, indigenous peoples, and community leaders to red-tagging, retaliation, or exclusion, and whether complaints and actions would be publicly reported.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog referred the human-rights question to the PNP/related official. The response cited a National Police Commission media-relations manual prohibiting red-tagging and said complaints could be brought to the Commission, which would act on them.

thread.speaker: Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: He asked for the objective criteria, allocations, accomplishment data, audit findings, delays, complaints, outcome evidence, and open-data disclosure supporting the proposed increase in SBDP.

thread.speaker: Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Mabilog said the apparent SBDP increase was misleading because more barangays would be covered. He said the allocation per barangay actually declined from 10,000,000 to 5,000,000, and referred again to DILG monitoring, its online platform, and CSO and NGO engagement.

topic: Barangay Development Program and SBDP per-barangay allocations
summary: Jose Teves Jr. pressed for a higher SBDP allocation, arguing that 5,000,000 per barangay was insufficient for classrooms, health centers, water, electrification, and other needs. DILG said it had requested 10,000,000 per barangay and would welcome a congressional increase to 7,000,000 or more. Members then sought delivery rates, audits, beneficiary verification, and third-party monitoring, while DILG reported delivery rates ranging from 29% to 100% across the cited years and said 700 monitoring personnel were deployed. Rep. Caroline Agyao obtained clarifications on EL CAC coverage and annual allocations, including 2,500,000 in 2025, 10,000,000 in 2026, and 5,000,000 proposed for 2027. DILG said municipalities implemented the projects, DILG monitored them, and coordination was intended to prevent duplication. A CSO representative questioned the rationale and accountability of the LGSF and SBDP, and DILG described three-tier monitoring, DBM vetting, grassroots consultations, and the SubayBayan portal. The hearing ended with document requests and commitments, while the adequacy of the 2027 allocation and the broader evidence supporting it remained open.
question: The committee sought to establish the appropriate per-barangay allocation for the Barangay Development Program/SBDP, the basis for changes in the proposed budget, and whether projects were properly selected, implemented, audited, monitored, and protected against duplication. Members and CSOs also asked what role DILG played in the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), what safeguards existed, and what documents and performance data would be submitted.
agency_position: DILG said the SBDP was a targeted program for barangays previously affected by communist armed groups, with projects selected through grassroots consultations and implemented by municipalities. It maintained that DILG's role was monitoring and evaluation, while DBM administered the LGSF and handled proposal vetting; DILG cited local, second-party, and third-party monitoring, the SubayBayan portal, and additional monitoring personnel as safeguards.
outcome: DILG acknowledged that the 2027 SBDP proposal provided only 5,000,000 per barangay despite DILG's request for 10,000,000, and members' calls for a higher amount were left to Congress. DILG committed to submit accomplishment, coverage, and third-party monitoring documents, but the requested independent outcome, audit, duplication, and open-data evidence was not fully supplied during the exchange.

positions.position: Supported increasing the SBDP allocation from 5,000,000 per barangay, preferably to 7,000,000 or more, because barangays faced substantial classroom, health, water, electrification, and other infrastructure needs.
Sought clarity on EL CAC coverage, the different annual per-barangay allocations, eligible projects, implementing agencies, and safeguards against duplication with DOH and other projects.
Pressed DILG for verified physical and financial accomplishment data, audits, beneficiary verification, and third-party monitoring reports.
Questioned the policy rationale, transparency, performance basis, community participation, safeguards, and independent accountability mechanisms for LGSF and SBDP.

topic: BFP fire-truck procurement, repair, stations, and emergency capacity
summary: Members repeatedly questioned DILG and the BFP about fire-truck shortages, station gaps, procurement corruption, repair and replacement, and emergency-response capacity. The agency said it was pursuing a government-to-government procurement with South Korea for about 1,500 trucks, with a maintenance contract and a stated cost advantage over prior purchases and Japan. Officials said BFP fire-code collections were remitted to the national treasury, while DBM released only about 1 billion annually, leaving the BFP with limited access to funds despite collections and earmarks totaling several billion pesos. Members cited municipalities without stations or trucks and shortages in protective equipment, while the BFP requested search-and-rescue trucks, ambulances, Unified 911 operating funds, and additional recruitment. The committee noted or supported possible trust-fund and appropriations action, and Rodriguez manifested an intent to seek approval of the requested increases. The Korea procurement remained under negotiation, with technical specifications and a written status update requested, so the issue landed as a supported but not fully resolved commitment.
question: The committee sought to establish how the BFP would finance, procure, maintain, and distribute fire trucks, rescue vehicles, ambulances, stations, and related equipment; how much it collected and actually received from fire-code fees; and whether the proposed government-to-government procurement with Korea would address national shortages. Members also asked about procurement safeguards, repair and replacement needs, station gaps, and emergency-response capacity.
agency_position: DILG and the BFP said procurement reforms and government-to-government purchasing, particularly with South Korea, would reduce corruption and lower unit costs while expanding the number of trucks acquired. They maintained that BFP fire-code collections were remitted to the national treasury but that DBM released only a limited portion, and asked Congress to support fuller use of the trust fund for trucks, stations, ambulances, rescue equipment, maintenance, and recruitment.
outcome: The committee generally supported the proposed Korea government-to-government procurement and the BFP's requests for additional trucks, stations, ambulances, rescue equipment, operating funds, and manpower. However, fuller access to fire-code collections, final procurement terms, supplier selection, and the requested budget increases remained dependent on congressional action, DBM releases, and further agency submissions.

topic: PNP additional funding, mobility, staffing, and regional equipment
summary: The chair presented the DILG's proposed budget of about 32.5 billion, including about 142.5 billion for the PNP, and linked public-safety funding to school security and law-enforcement capability. Mark Huanko supported the DILG budget but pressed for implementation of the Lingayen road project, recovery of disputed PNP property, and replacement of aging vehicles; the PNP committed to act, investigate, coordinate, and report back. The agency said 95% of the Mahindra vehicles acquired in 2010 and 2011 were beyond economic repair, and Huanko requested 231 vehicles for the district's 231 barangays. Mica Gonzales asked about recruitment into violence and permanent police presence near schools, and the agency said sensitive details could be discussed in executive session while school police presence was already policy. Rufus Rodriguez cited Region 10 mobility deliveries and supported additional PNP funding; the PNP chief confirmed an additional request of 2,025,000,000 after initially stating conflicting figures. A majority member also raised DILG field-office staffing shortages, and the agency said a government optimization plan was being prepared.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the DILG and PNP had sufficient funding, vehicles, personnel, and regional equipment to meet public-safety needs. Members also asked about the implementation of a Lingayen police-road project, recovery of disputed PNP property, school-area police deployment, and proposed staffing increases for DILG field offices.
agency_position: The DILG and PNP supported additional operational capacity through vehicles, capital outlays, recruitment, school-area police presence, and field-office staffing. The PNP committed to pursuing the Lingayen road and property matters, accounting for vehicle needs, updating the member, augmenting police forces in the next recruitment or fiscal-year cycle, and seeking an additional request identified as 2,025,000,000.
outcome: The hearing produced agency commitments on the Lingayen road and property matters, vehicle accounting, police augmentation, school-area deployment, and a field-office optimization plan. The PNP additional request was identified as 2,025,000,000, but final congressional action on that request and the vehicle allocations remained subject to the budget process.

topic: School-violence prevention, active-shooter drills, and school police presence
summary: The Chair and several members raised concerns about school violence, online recruitment into violence, firearms used by minors, and the need for faster police response. DILG and PNP officials said police were already present during school entry and dismissal and that barangay tanods would be allowed inside schools under a joint memorandum circular. Officials reported 50 school-related incidents involving minors, a 97% five-minute 911 response compliance rate, and a PNP operations increase of about 15 billion. The agencies proposed nationwide active-attack drills with DepEd, a youth ambassadors program, coordination with DICT and NTC on malicious online sites, and expanded Unified 911 vehicles. The Secretary also proposed stricter firearm-safekeeping inspections and penalties, while members questioned the emphasis on video games and stressed broader social and mental-health factors. The agencies committed to refine and submit drill guidelines, but the hearing left the definite schedule, dedicated budget line, and firearm-enforcement data unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish what DILG, the PNP, DepEd, LGUs, and attached agencies were budgeting and implementing to prevent school violence, monitor online recruitment into violence, secure firearms, conduct active-attack drills, and ensure rapid police response. Members also asked whether police presence near schools could be made permanent or assigned to individual schools.

The PNP reported 97% compliance with a five-minute response target for 911 calls, but officials did not identify a dedicated school-drill budget line or provide all requested firearm-enforcement data.
outcome: The hearing established a package of planned or ongoing measures—school police presence, barangay tanod augmentation, DepEd coordination, active-attack drills, online-site coordination, firearm-safekeeping reforms, and expanded emergency response. The committee did not receive a separate school-drill budget line, a definite drill date, or the requested firearm-license enforcement counts, leaving implementation and funding details open.

topic: Firearms control, safekeeping, and police use of firearms
summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula, Rep. Rolando Valeriano, Rep. Edgar Erice, Renee Co, Rep. Robert Raymond Estrella, and Anna York Bondoc questioned the DILG and PNP about firearm safekeeping, loose firearms, mobilization protocols, and school safety. The agency said 800,000 uniformed personnel were covered by firearm-responsibility rules, but acknowledged that firearms in the Tacloban and Zamboanga incidents had not been properly secured. Officials proposed advance-notice PNP inspections of lawful firearm owners' homes, stronger penalties for irresponsible safekeeping, and repeal of the Robin Padilla law; they repeatedly cited 98% as the share of firearm violence or firearm-related cases involving loose or unlicensed firearms. The PNP said it had only 2,000 body cameras for 320,000 personnel and was procuring another 10 or 20,000, while acknowledging that firearms carried during mobilizations may have reflected a mistake. For school security, officials cited barangay tanods, police coordination, active-attack drills, online-platform coordination, and community participation, but said assigning police to each of about 56,000 schools was impractical. The committee requested reports on the mobilizations, the Zamboanga mistaken-identity case, and the DILG's firearm-regulation recommendations; data on license suspensions and related cases was not supplied.
question: The committee sought to establish how the DILG and PNP were preventing firearms from being misused, particularly firearms issued to uniformed personnel or legally owned by civilians. Members also asked about controls during police mobilizations, penalties for irresponsible safekeeping, school security, and whether additional enforcement, inspection, identification, and accountability measures were needed.
agency_position: The DILG and PNP said firearm owners and custodians were responsible for secure safekeeping, but acknowledged that the two school-shooting incidents reflected failures in that responsibility. They supported revising the IRR to permit advance-notice inspections of firearm storage, imposing stronger penalties for irresponsible or illegal possession, and repealing the Robin Padilla law to make loose-firearm offenses non-bailable. They also maintained that school security required coordinated police, barangay, education, and community measures rather than a dedicated police officer for every school.
outcome: The agency's proposals for IRR amendments, home inspections, stronger penalties, and repeal of the Robin Padilla law were presented but were not enacted during the hearing. The committee requested investigative and policy documents, while the requested statistics on firearm-related license suspensions and cases remained unanswered.

DILG and PNP officials said local governments should address many frontline services within their budgets and committed to corrective or enforcement action on personnel-related violence and insensitive materials. The NCMF later reported inadequate Hajj medical funding, citing 95 pesos per pilgrim from a spoken allocation of 600 16,000 pesos, and requested support for three priority programs. topic: BFP recruitment integrity, manpower, and personnel needs
summary: Perci Cendaña raised alleged BFP recruitment slot-selling and sought clarification on the agency's controls. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said prior slot prices ranged from 200,000 to 800,000 per slot and referred the matter to the BFP chief, who described the online e-hiring system and confirmed a recent Region Three entrapment operation involving recruitment anomalies. The BFP said future recruitment would be fair, transparent, and based on merit and fitness. The chief reported that DBM provided about 2,000 recruits annually against a stated ideal manpower requirement of about 78,000; the transcript also gave an authorized strength of 43, with the unit unclear. He said the current rate would require twenty years and sought an additional 2,000 recruits per year. The Chair welcomed the agency action, but no approval of the additional recruitment request was recorded.

It committed to fair, transparent, merit- and fitness-based recruitment, while stating that the agency needed more than the 2,000 recruits currently provided annually to address its manpower shortfall.
outcome: The BFP confirmed that a recruitment anomaly had been exposed and acted on, and the Chair accepted the explanation that the matter had reached the bureau. The broader request for additional annual recruitment remained an agency appeal rather than a recorded committee approval.

topic: Youth programs, NYC budget, and ICT modernization
summary: A committee member questioned the NYC's proposed budget reduction of about 19,000,000 and the omission of requests for Muslim and creative youth summits and ICT modernization. The NYC explained the summit proposals and identified an ICT request of 24,000,948, while acknowledging that only two people handled procurement and that additional personnel-services funding was needed to absorb more funds. Jambaronda also sought broader SK training and compliance, leading DILG to commit to revisiting modules and issuing further guidance. Members additionally requested active-shooter-drill guidelines and information on political-dynasty recommendations, with agencies undertaking to submit or obtain the requested materials. The budget increase itself remained unapproved in the transcript.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the National Youth Commission's reduced 2027 budget could support its expanding youth mandate, including Muslim and creative youth summits, ICT modernization, youth mental-health and entrepreneurship programs, SK training, and services for out-of-school youth. Members also sought specific agency commitments, data, and interagency coordination on youth safety and political-dynasty concerns.
agency_position: The NYC said its youth mandate was primarily advocacy, policy, coordination, and capacity building, while acknowledging that its budget and staffing constrained implementation and absorptive capacity. It supported additional funding and personnel services, particularly for ICT modernization, youth entrepreneurship, SK training, research, and expanded youth programs, but said it lacked police power and certain data, which required coordination with DILG, DepEd, COMELEC, and other agencies.
outcome: The NYC budget issue was not finally resolved: the committee chair expressed support for restoration or increases, while the NYC acknowledged both unmet program requests and staffing-related absorptive-capacity limits. The committee obtained commitments for additional documents, revised SK guidance, active-shooter-drill guidelines, and follow-up with COMELEC.

Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla committed to an immediate memorandum circular on annual development plans and said noncompliant local governments could be excluded from the SGLG; he also took note of the request to regulate barangay travel. Rep. Bambi Mano asked whether DILG could hear and correct an appeal from an SK chair's dismissal, and the DILG undersecretary answered that it could under section 67 of the Local Government Code and the SK-related laws, subject to a written follow-up. The NYC described continuing SK training, auditing guidance, trainer-of-trainers arrangements, and an MOU with local government accountants, while DILG committed to revisit the one-day orientation modules. The NYC reported a training estimate of roughly 70 plus million, with the transcript also recording 72,000,000,000, and said a survey of 120 federation presidents was examining support for an extension or special elections. The agencies agreed to issue further guidance and submit information, but election timing, removal data, and out-of-school youth data remained open.
question: The committee sought to establish whether SK and barangay officials were receiving adequate training, complying with planning and fiscal requirements, and subject to effective oversight and removal procedures. It also sought clarification on DILG's appellate authority over SK dismissals, the timing of SK elections or special elections, and the reliability of out-of-school youth data.
agency_position: DILG maintained that it had appellate authority to resolve an appeal from an SK chair's dismissal under section 67 of the Local Government Code and that dismissal propriety could also be considered under Republic Act 10742 and the SK Reform Law of 2015. The NYC and DILG supported expanded training, auditing guidance, and compliance monitoring, but the NYC said it could encourage SK compliance rather than mandate it and deferred removal questions to DILG.
outcome: The hearing produced commitments for memorandum circulars, enhanced SK orientation and training, additional compliance guidance, submission of SK membership figures, and possible NYC research funding. DILG answered the appellate-authority question affirmatively, but the dismissal case remained subject to the submission and review of Rep. Mano's documents; the election timing and reliable out-of-school youth figures were not resolved.

topic: Disaster preparedness, LGU capacity, and flood rescue
summary: The chair and members linked disaster resilience and LGU capacity to the DILG budget, citing 50,441 evacuation centers and more than 126,000 deployed uniformed personnel. Teves questioned BFP capital outlay and rescue capacity, while Remulla attributed the earlier reduction to procurement reforms and pointed to planned acquisitions, including 1,500 trucks through a government-to-government transaction. topic: Seal of Good Local Governance validation and compliance
summary: Rep. Edgar Erice challenged whether the SGLG measured actual governance outcomes or merely documentary compliance. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the DILG had moved to a whole-of-term assessment, reducing the former 10 indicators and as many as 14 categories to resiliency, fiscal management, and innovation; he cited 5,000,000 man hours previously spent annually and an estimated 5,000,000,000 cost for full third-party validation. Erice proposed using an appropriations provision to fund third-party validation, which the secretary welcomed. Rep. Sergio Dagooc asked that electric-bill compliance be added to fiscal-management criteria, and the secretary committed to include it in the next evaluation. In response to Rep. Jambaranda, the secretary committed to an immediate memorandum circular requiring annual development plans and excluding noncompliant LGUs from the SGLG. The request to regulate barangay travel orders was noted but not resolved.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) measured actual improvements in local services and governance, rather than merely documentary compliance. Members also asked whether third-party validation and additional fiscal-management criteria could be incorporated into the SGLG.
agency_position: The DILG said the SGLG had been redesigned as a whole-of-term assessment rather than an annual checklist, with three principal indicators: resiliency, fiscal management, and innovation. The agency supported third-party validation if Congress provided funding and committed to include an electric-bill criterion in the next evaluation and to issue a memorandum circular linking annual development-plan submission to SGLG eligibility.
outcome: The agency answered that the SGLG had been shifted to a whole-of-term, three-area assessment and accepted the possibility of third-party validation if Congress funded it. It also undertook specific follow-up measures on electric-bill compliance and annual development plans, while travel regulation and broader SK concerns remained open.

topic: Solid-waste management and LGU contract oversight
summary: Jose Teves Jr. asked who was responsible for overseeing LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the Local Government Code assigned waste disposal to municipalities and cities, producing fragmented and potentially inefficient systems, and proposed a regional approach. Rep. Edgar Erice later tied the issue to Metro Manila's 14,000,000 residents and 12,000 metric tons of daily garbage, asking whether DILG could use its general-supervision authority to review LGU contracts. Remulla said DILG had no supervisory power over those contracts and identified COWA as the responsible body as rendered in the transcript. He maintained that the Local Government Code should be revisited because regionalized collection would be more effective than detailed supervision of 40,000 LGUs. The issue remained unresolved, with no specific legal change or oversight mechanism adopted.
question: The committee sought to establish which level or agency was responsible for ensuring LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003 and whether DILG could exercise supervisory authority over LGU garbage-collection contracts. Members also examined whether the current LGU-by-LGU system was adequate for the scale of waste and flooding problems, particularly in Metro Manila.
agency_position: DILG said it did not have supervisory power over LGU contracts, identifying COWA as the office with that authority as rendered in the transcript. Secretary Remulla argued that the central problem was the LGU-by-LGU structure required by the Local Government Code and supported revisiting the law to establish a more integrated, regional system with clearer accountability and oversight.
outcome: The agency answered that DILG could not oversee LGU contracts under its current authority and proposed structural and legal reform toward regional garbage management. The committee did not adopt a specific amendment, assign a new oversight agency, or resolve the contract-supervision issue during the hearing.

positions.position: He sought clear oversight of LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations and agreed that the applicable legal framework should be revisited.
He argued that the scale of Metro Manila's waste and flooding problems required an accountable agency with authority to examine LGU garbage contracts and support an integrated metropolitan approach.
He supported regionalizing garbage management and changing the Local Government Code rather than relying on DILG's existing general-supervision authority to conduct detailed contract oversight.

topic: PNP accountability, body cameras, and public-assembly operations
summary: Jose Teves Jr. raised PNP oversight and anti-hazing accountability, while DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla reported that NAPOCOM had cleared a backlog of about 15,000 cases and had no remaining backlog. Renee Co questioned arrests during mobilizations, police firearms, and the reported more than 700,000 Safer Cities apprehensions. The secretary defended the arrests and initiative but acknowledged that the PNP had only 2,000 body-worn cameras for 320,000 personnel, with another 10 or 20,000 being procured, and said crime reductions ranged from about 30% to 60% depending on the category. The member also challenged the agency’s explanation of school violence and raised arbitrary barangay-level drug-watch listings; officials cited intelligence procedures, supply-and-demand reduction, and operational safeguards. The agency agreed to provide operation reports, incident logs, updated statistics, and a disciplinary report, with the latter committed for submission on Tuesday. The broader questions about firearms, arrests, and enforcement safeguards remained contested.
question: The committee sought to establish whether PNP arrests and public-assembly operations complied with human-rights and public-assembly rules, including restrictions on firearms and requirements for body-worn cameras. Members also sought the factual basis and safeguards for the Safer Cities Initiative, the agency’s approach to school violence and drug-watch listings, and the status of police-accountability cases and reports.
agency_position: The DILG and its police-accountability officials maintained that arrests were based on vandalism or aggression, that firearms were not drawn or used against rally participants, and that the Safer Cities Initiative did not violate constitutional rights. The agency acknowledged obsolete and insufficient body-worn-camera equipment, defended its intelligence and drug-enforcement procedures, reported zero NAPOCOM backlog, and undertook to submit operation, incident, statistical, and disciplinary documents.
outcome: The agency defended its arrest and enforcement practices but acknowledged deficient body-camera coverage and left the legality and proportionality concerns contested. It committed to investigate and submit operational, statistical, and disciplinary records, with the disciplinary report specifically set for Tuesday; the broader accountability questions were not fully resolved during the hearing.

positions.position: Supported stronger PNP supervision, discipline, and accountability, and sought enforcement and resolution of anti-hazing cases.

Questioned the legality and proportionality of mobilization arrests, police firearms, Safer Cities apprehensions, and drug-watch listings. She pressed for functional body cameras, documentary support, safeguards for children and student leaders, and a broader explanation of school violence.
Defended the agency’s operations while acknowledging equipment deficiencies and arguing that the Safer Cities Initiative reduced crime without violating constitutional rights.

topic: LGSF and local-project implementation safeguards
summary: Rep. Miro Quimbo raised recurring building-permit delays that had stranded local projects, especially schools and health facilities, and DILG agreed to examine specific cases after receiving data. A member then asked DILG and the PNP to distinguish excavation from quarrying and clarify heavy-equipment impoundment; DILG said local governments generally lacked that authority, while the PNP said it enforced violations in coordination with the DENR and LGUs. A CSO representative questioned the rationale for retaining LGSF despite an estimated national tax allocation of about 1.32 to 1.4 billion trillion pesos, and DILG defended the roughly 58 billion fund as additional support for local basic services. DILG said DBM handled proposal vetting while DILG monitored implementation through technical personnel, three-tier monitoring, and the SubayBayan portal. Members also sought safeguards against duplicate projects, weak participation, red-tagging, and ineffective implementation, while DILG and NAPOLCOM described existing monitoring and complaint mechanisms. DILG said the proposed SBDP allocation of about 9.74 billion actually reduced the per-barangay amount to 5,000,000 because coverage expanded to 1,904 barangays, leaving several requests for supporting evidence and public accountability information unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish how DILG would use its supervisory and monitoring powers to address delayed building permits, stranded local projects, and questionable local enforcement actions. It also examined the policy rationale, safeguards, monitoring responsibilities, and proposed funding levels for the Local Government Support Fund and related programs.
agency_position: DILG maintained that compliant building-permit applications should not be delayed and undertook to examine specific cases. It said local governments identified and procured LGSF projects, DBM handled proposal vetting and validation, and DILG monitored implementation through deployed technical personnel, three-tier monitoring, and the SubayBayan portal. DILG also defended LGSF and SBDP as additional resources for local basic services, while the PNP and NAPOLCOM described enforcement and red-tagging safeguards.
outcome: DILG answered the committee's questions in general terms and undertook to examine the building-permit and local-enforcement cases after receiving supporting details. The LGSF and SBDP safeguards and allocations were explained, but questions about independent validation, public reporting, outcome evidence, and the adequacy of funding remained open.

positions.position: Delayed or overly technical building-permit requirements were stranding locally implemented projects and required DILG intervention and possible administrative action.
Local authorities needed clear guidance on the distinction between excavation and quarrying and on whether they could impound heavy equipment.

The committee needed clearer accountability for LGSF proposal validation, duplicate-project prevention, community participation, monitoring outputs, and the justification for proposed program allocations.
The continued existence and scale of LGSF required policy justification given the increased national tax allotment, along with safeguards against duplication and exclusion.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo raised recurring delays in building permits for projects funded under programs in 2025 and 2026, saying additional requirements were sometimes imposed after compliance. He said the delays had stranded projects, particularly schools and health facilities, and asked what recourse was available.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official said building-permit requirements were already set and that a permit should be issued when a project proponent faithfully complied with all requirements.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo replied that local officials sometimes applied fine nuances to requirements, such as location plans, in ways that went beyond what was reasonable. He said the matter required DILG attention through its supervisory powers over local governments.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The official undertook to look into the concern raised by Rep. Quimbo.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo said he would provide the available data and asked whether cases involving regular employees who refused building-permit applications could warrant disciplinary or administrative proceedings.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The official asked Rep. Quimbo to provide additional details so DILG could determine the proper course of action.

thread.speaker: Rep. Miro Quimbo
thread.said: Rep. Quimbo said, “I will hold you to that,” referring to the DILG undertaking to examine the matter.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: A member asked DILG and the police to clarify the distinction between excavation and quarrying and whether a task force or provincial government could impound heavy equipment involved in local development activities. The member said a letter on the issue had been received by Secretary Vince Dizon and would also be furnished to the agencies.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member tested the distinction by asking whether canal work, reblocking, and clearing landslides constituted quarrying or excavation.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official classified canal work, reblocking, and landslide clearing generally as excavation, provided the activity was not illegal or prohibited by existing law.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member pressed for a yes-or-no answer on whether local governments were authorized to impound the equipment.

thread.speaker: a DILG official
thread.said: The DILG official said the authority to impound was not vested in the local government unit.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member described a local situation involving a task force and police action on private land and a fish pond and asked for guidance on what should be done.

thread.speaker: PNP official
thread.said: The PNP official said police must enforce the law when heavy machinery is used in illegal excavation or quarrying activities in violation of special laws, DENR laws, or local ordinances.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member asked whether the police acted as deputized enforcers of the DENR.

thread.speaker: PNP official
thread.said: The PNP official agreed, explaining that enforcement was undertaken in coordination with the appropriate agency, including the DENR and the local government.

thread.speaker: a member
thread.said: The member was advised to provide an intelligence report or other details so the matter could be investigated. The member said copies would be furnished to DILG and the PNP and asked DILG to examine the issue through its supervisory powers over local governments.

thread.speaker: CSO representative
thread.said: The CSO representative asked why a separate LGSF should be retained when the Mandanas-Garcia ruling had increased the national tax allotment of local governments. The representative also asked what fiscal gaps LGSF addressed and how the government prevented duplication or substitution of regular LGU resources.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said the national tax allotment appeared large but had to be divided among all provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays and was insufficient for LGU priority projects and devolved functions. He said the LGSF provided additional resources for water and sanitation systems, farm-to-market roads, electrification, health centers, and other basic services.

thread.speaker: CSO representative
thread.said: The CSO representative asked what role DILG played in LGSF implementation, particularly whether it vetted and validated project proposals.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said LGSF was released directly to LGUs, while DILG monitored, evaluated, and checked implementation. He said DILG deployed engineers and project evaluation officers to provinces and regions.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked whether validation and vetting of proposals were handled by the Department of Budget and Management.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog confirmed that LGUs submitted proposals through a DBM-created portal. Rep. Fuentebella noted that DBM, rather than DILG, handled the vetting and validation relevant to preventing duplicate projects.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked what measurable outputs, disclosure requirements, accountability mechanisms, and CSO participation would accompany DILG's monitoring and evaluation allocation for LGSF projects.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog described a three-tier monitoring system: local project monitoring committees composed of LGU officials and CSOs, DILG's second-party monitoring, and third-party monitoring involving CSOs and nongovernmental organizations. He also cited the SubayBayan portal for required project status updates.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked about the relative allocations for LGSF, participatory budgeting, and the Support to Barangay Development Program, and how DILG would expand meaningful community and CSO participation.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said the Support to Barangay Development Program addressed basic-service gaps in barangays previously influenced by communist armed groups and used grassroots consultations to identify projects. He said the participatory budgeting fund supported water systems and evacuation centers in identified municipalities.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked what safeguards and grievance mechanisms protected CSOs, human-rights defenders, Indigenous Peoples, community leaders, and other stakeholders from red-tagging, retaliation, or exclusion in LGSF and SBDP implementation.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog referred the red-tagging question to the National Police Commission.

thread.speaker: National Police Commission official
thread.said: The official said a recently issued media-relations manual prohibited red-tagging and provided for sanctions. The official said the National Police Commission would accept and act on complaints.

thread.speaker: Rep. Arnie Fuentebella
thread.said: Rep. Fuentebella asked for the evidence supporting the proposed increase in SBDP funding, including beneficiary-selection criteria, allocations, accomplishment rates, audit findings, delays, complaints, outcome evidence, and publication of project-level data.

thread.speaker: DILG Undersecretary Jed Mabilog
thread.said: Undersecretary Mabilog said the apparent SBDP increase actually reduced the allocation per barangay because more barangays were covered. He said DILG's existing monitoring, evaluation, portal, and CSO/NGO engagement mechanisms were intended to ensure faithful implementation.

topic: NCMF Hajj medical expenses and priority programs
summary: Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula raised the adequacy of the NCMF's Hajj operations and medical budget for 2027. The NCMF said its medical allocation was only 600 16,000 pesos, or 95 pesos per projected pilgrim for 6,000 pilgrims, and sought an increase to 6,100,000. The agency also identified three priority programs: Madaris at 87,500,000, the Halal and Muslim community economic empowerment program at the unclear figure "89.04 94,000,000," and Hajj operation modernization at 6,100,000; it stated a total of 24,000,537. A committee member asked for the written request and said the request would be supported and advocated. Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula separately manifested full support for the NCMF budget, but the transcript did not establish final approval of any additional amount.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the NCMF's proposed 2027 budget adequately covered Hajj operations and medical needs for the projected pilgrims. It also asked which NCMF priority programs required additional consideration or funding.
agency_position: The NCMF stated that the proposed medical allocation for Hajj operations was inadequate, providing only 95 pesos per projected pilgrim, and sought an increase. It asked the House to consider its three priority programs—Madaris, the Halal industry and Muslim community economic empowerment program, and Hajj operation modernization—if the full request could not be approved.
outcome: The NCMF's request for additional Hajj medical funding and consideration of its priority programs was supported in principle. The agency was instructed to submit its written request, and a committee member undertook to advocate for it; approval of the requested amounts was not established.
